vignette:
He is twenty-four years old, a QA engineer for a mid-size software firm, and he has been coming to therapy for six weeks now, though he still sits on the edge of the chair, coat on, keys in hand. His name is Miguel. He is Latin American, the youngest of three brothers, the only one who stayed in the city after college. He lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment near the office, and most days he cannot bring himself to open the blinds.

Miguel does not talk about the fire right away. He talks about the project he is testing-a customer-facing dashboard for a retail client-and how he keeps finding bugs that his team says are not real. He reruns the same test scripts three, four times. He checks the logs, the timestamps, the stack traces. He sees patterns that are not there. His supervisor told him last week that he is "overthinking it." Miguel knows he is right, though. He can feel it. Something is wrong, something will fail, and when it does, people will get hurt.

The fire happened eighteen months ago. He was working late with three other engineers in a converted warehouse the company used as a secondary office. It was a "hackathon night"-pizza, energy drinks, folding tables covered in monitors. Around 2 a.m. someone smelled smoke. A faulty power strip under a server rack had caught fire, and within minutes the ceiling tiles were melting. He remembers the sound more than anything: a low, wet hiss, then the fire alarm, then a woman screaming his name. He climbed over a fallen table to reach the exit. He does not remember his own hands pushing the door open. He remembers the cold air outside, the sirens, and his coworker Linda sitting on the curb with a gash on her arm, crying. He did not go home for three days. He stayed at a hotel and ran the sequence over and over: the smell, the scream, the dark hallway. He could not stop seeing the faces of the other people inside.

Since then, his sleep has become a series of small collapses. He goes to bed around 2 a.m. after checking the stove, the space heater, the phone charger, the smart plug-everything plugged into a surge protector he bought the day after the fire. He lies down, and his brain replays that night without permission. He sees the orange light under the door, feels the heat on his neck. Sometimes he jerks awake before he can get out. More often he stays in bed, staring at the ceiling, running the escape route from his apartment over and over: door, stairwell, street, corner. He has done it so many times he could draw it blindfolded.

At work, Miguel avoids the break room. That is the hardest part, because it is the only place with a window. But the break room smells faintly of burnt coffee, and the smell is too close. He eats lunch at his desk with his headphones on, white noise loud enough to cover the sound of the HVAC kicking on. He has stopped going to the weekly team stand-up because it is held in a conference room with a single door and no sprinkler. He tells his manager he has "developer conflicts." He knows it sounds like an excuse. It is an excuse.

He does not go to bars or parties anymore. His brother invited him to a backyard barbecue last month and he agreed, but when he arrived and saw a grill with flames licking the grate, he turned around without speaking to anyone and drove home. He called in sick the next day. He has lost track of how many times he has done that.

The PCL-5 score from his intake was 56. He read the number on the printout and felt something cold settle in his chest. He knows the number is a score. He does not know what it means, except that it is high. He looks younger than twenty-four when he talks about it-a boy who still expects the world to be safe, and is angry that it is not. He keeps saying he just wants to get back to normal, but normal is a place he cannot find the address for. He is not sure it exists anymore.
